source: IAU constellation list; stories are short original summaries written for this app

constellations.name: Andromeda
constellations.story: Princess Andromeda was chained to a rock as a sacrifice to the sea monster Cetus and rescued by Perseus. The constellation is best known for M31, the Andromeda Galaxy, the nearest large spiral galaxy and the most distant object most people can see with the naked eye. Its brightest star, Alpheratz, is shared with the corner of the Great Square of Pegasus.

constellations.name: Antlia
constellations.story: Antlia is the Air Pump, one of the faint southern constellations named by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 1750s after a scientific instrument. It contains no star brighter than fourth magnitude, and its brightest, Alpha Antliae, is a cool orange giant. The constellation is a quiet patch of the southern sky with little to catch the eye.

constellations.name: Apus
constellations.story: Apus is the Bird of Paradise, a southern constellation introduced by Dutch navigators at the end of the 16th century. Its name comes from the Greek word 'apous', meaning footless, because early Europeans believed birds of paradise never landed. It lies near the south celestial pole and contains only faint stars, the brightest being Alpha Apodis.

constellations.name: Aquarius
constellations.story: Aquarius is the Water Bearer, an ancient zodiac constellation often linked to Ganymede, the youth Zeus brought to Olympus to pour the gods' drinks. Its stars are drawn as a figure pouring water from a jar into the mouth of Piscis Austrinus, the southern fish. The constellation contains the Helix Nebula, one of the nearest bright planetary nebulae, and the globular cluster M2.

constellations.name: Aquila
constellations.story: Aquila is the Eagle, the bird of Zeus that carried his thunderbolts in Greek myth. Its brightest star, Altair, forms one corner of the Summer Triangle with Vega and Deneb, and it spins so fast that it is visibly flattened. Two fainter stars, Tarazed and Alshain, mark the eagle's outstretched wings.

constellations.name: Ara
constellations.story: Ara is the Altar, where the gods swore their alliance before the war against the Titans. It lies in a rich part of the southern Milky Way and holds NGC 6397, one of the closest globular clusters to Earth. Its brightest star, Beta Arae, is an orange supergiant about 650 light-years away.

constellations.name: Aries
constellations.story: Aries is the Ram with the Golden Fleece, the prize sought by Jason and the Argonauts. It was once home to the vernal equinox, the point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator, and that point is still called the First Point of Aries even though precession has moved it into Pisces. Its brightest star is Hamal, an orange giant.

constellations.name: Auriga
constellations.story: Auriga is the Charioteer, often identified with Erichthonius, the Athenian king who invented the four-horse chariot. Its brightest star, Capella, is a system of four stars that looks like a single golden point and is the sixth-brightest star in the night sky. The constellation also contains the open clusters M36, M37 and M38.

constellations.name: Boötes
constellations.story: The Herdsman is a figure said to drive the bears around the pole, and the constellation's kite shape is easy to find once Arcturus is spotted. Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere, a red giant only about 37 light-years away. Following the curve of the Big Dipper's handle leads the eye straight to it.

constellations.name: Caelum
constellations.story: Caelum is the Chisel, a small and faint southern constellation introduced by Lacaille in the 18th century to honour the sculptor's tools. It has no star brighter than fourth magnitude. Alpha Caeli, the brightest, is a yellow-white star about 66 light-years away.

constellations.name: Camelopardalis
constellations.story: Camelopardalis is the Giraffe, a large but faint northern constellation created by Petrus Plancius in the early 17th century. Its name blends 'camel' and 'leopard', an old European way of describing a giraffe. It contains the spiral galaxy IC 342, which is large and bright but hidden behind dust in the Milky Way.

constellations.name: Cancer
constellations.story: Cancer is the Crab, the crab sent by Hera to distract Heracles during his fight with the Hydra. It is the faintest of the zodiac constellations, yet it contains M44, the Beehive Cluster, a large open star cluster visible to the naked eye under dark skies. Its brightest star is Tarf, an orange giant.

constellations.name: Canes Venatici
constellations.story: Canes Venatici is the Hunting Dogs, introduced by Johannes Hevelius in the 17th century to represent the two dogs held by the Herdsman. Its brightest star, Cor Caroli, was named in honour of King Charles of England. The constellation contains the Whirlpool Galaxy M51 and the Sunflower Galaxy M63.

constellations.name: Canis Major
constellations.story: Canis Major is the Great Dog, the larger of Orion's two hunting dogs and home to Sirius, the brightest star in Earth's night sky. Sirius is a blue-white star only 8.6 light-years away, with a faint white-dwarf companion called Sirius B. The constellation also contains the open cluster M41 and the bright blue star Adhara.

constellations.name: Canis Minor
constellations.story: Canis Minor is the Little Dog, the smaller of Orion's two hunting dogs, marked mainly by two stars. Its brightest, Procyon, is one of the closest stars to the Sun and forms the Winter Triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse. Procyon is a binary, with a faint white-dwarf companion.

constellations.name: Capricornus
constellations.story: Capricornus is the Sea Goat, a goat with a fish's tail, often linked to the god Pan, who jumped into the Nile to escape the monster Typhon. It is a faint zodiac constellation whose brightest star is Deneb Algedi, an eclipsing binary. The Sun passes through Capricornus from late January to mid-February.

constellations.name: Carina
constellations.story: Carina is the Keel, the largest piece of the old constellation Argo Navis, the ship of the Argonauts, which was broken up in the 18th century. It contains Canopus, the second-brightest star in the night sky, and the unstable supergiant Eta Carinae, which erupted in the 1840s and is now wrapped in the Homunculus Nebula. The constellation also holds the young open clusters NGC 3532 and IC 2602.

constellations.name: Cassiopeia
constellations.story: Cassiopeia is the Queen, the boastful mother of Andromeda, condemned to circle the pole on her throne. Its five brightest stars form a distinctive W or M shape, and from most northern latitudes the constellation never sets. It contains Tycho's supernova of 1572, the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, and the open clusters M52 and M103.

constellations.name: Centaurus
constellations.story: Centaurus is the Centaur, generally identified with Chiron, the wise teacher of Greek heroes. Its brightest star, Rigil Kentaurus, is the nearest star system to the Sun at 4.3 light-years, and its neighbour Hadar belongs to the same group. The constellation contains Omega Centauri, the largest and brightest globular cluster in the Milky Way.

constellations.name: Cepheus
constellations.story: Cepheus is the King, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda. Its stars form a house with a peaked roof, and it contains Delta Cephei, the prototype of the Cepheid variable stars used to measure distances across the galaxy. It also contains Mu Cephei, the Garnet Star, one of the largest stars known.

constellations.name: Cetus
constellations.story: Cetus is the Sea Monster, the creature sent to devour Andromeda and defeated by Perseus. It is a large constellation on the celestial equator that includes Mira, the first variable star ever recognised, which brightens and fades over about 11 months. Cetus also contains M77, a bright face-on spiral galaxy.

constellations.name: Chamaeleon
constellations.story: Chamaeleon is a small southern constellation named for the colour-changing lizard and introduced by Dutch navigators in the 1590s. It lies near the south celestial pole and has no bright stars, only a scattering of third- and fourth-magnitude suns. The constellation contains the Chamaeleon dark clouds, a nearby complex where new stars are forming.

constellations.name: Circinus
constellations.story: Circinus is the Compass, a small southern constellation introduced by Lacaille in the 18th century to represent the draftsman's compass. It sits beside Alpha Centauri but has no star brighter than third magnitude. It contains the Circinus Galaxy, an active spiral galaxy partly hidden behind the Milky Way.

constellations.name: Columba
constellations.story: Columba is the Dove, a small southern constellation placed just below Orion by Petrus Plancius in 1592. It is often identified with Noah's dove or with the dove that guided the Argonauts through the Clashing Rocks. Its brightest star is Phact, a blue-white subgiant.

constellations.name: Coma Berenices
constellations.story: Coma Berenices is Berenice's Hair, named for Queen Berenice II of Egypt, who cut off her hair as an offering to Aphrodite for her husband's safe return. It is one of the few constellations named after a historical person, and it contains the Coma Cluster, a huge cluster of galaxies. The north galactic pole lies within its borders, and so does M64, the Black Eye Galaxy.

constellations.name: Corona Australis
constellations.story: Corona Australis is the Southern Crown, a small arc of stars below the Teapot of Sagittarius that was known to Ptolemy. It lies along the Milky Way and contains one of the closest star-forming regions to Earth, the Corona Australis molecular cloud. Its brightest stars are only about fourth magnitude.

constellations.name: Corona Borealis
constellations.story: Corona Borealis is the Northern Crown, the jewelled crown Ariadne threw into the sky after her wedding to Dionysus. Its seven brightest stars form a neat semicircle, and its brightest, Alphecca, is an eclipsing binary. The constellation also contains R Coronae Borealis, a star that occasionally dims dramatically.

constellations.name: Corvus
constellations.story: Corvus is the Crow, the bird Apollo sent to fetch water in the cup Crater. It lingered at a fig tree and lied about a water snake, so Apollo placed it in the sky with the cup just out of reach. Its four main stars form a compact quadrilateral south of Virgo, and the constellation contains the Antennae Galaxies, two colliding spirals.

constellations.name: Crater
constellations.story: Crater is the Cup, the goblet of Apollo, placed beside the crow Corvus and the water snake Hydra. It is a faint constellation with no star brighter than third magnitude; its brightest is Delta Crateris, an orange giant. Its stars form a small group shaped like a cup on Hydra's back.

constellations.name: Crux
constellations.story: Crux is the Southern Cross, the smallest constellation and the one that appears on several southern national flags. It was not known to the ancient Greeks as a separate constellation; it was carved out of the hind legs of Centaurus in the 16th century. It points the way to the south celestial pole and contains the dark Coalsack Nebula as well as the bright stars Acrux and Mimosa.

constellations.name: Cygnus
constellations.story: Cygnus is the Swan, often identified with Zeus in disguise or with the mourning friend of Phaethon. Its brightest stars form the Northern Cross, with Deneb at the top, and Deneb is one of the most luminous stars visible to the naked eye. The constellation contains the Veil Nebula, the remnant of an ancient supernova, the double star Albireo, and Cygnus X-1, the first widely accepted black hole.

constellations.name: Delphinus
constellations.story: Delphinus is the Dolphin, the sea creature that persuaded the nymph Amphitrite to marry Poseidon. It is a tiny constellation whose compact diamond of stars looks like a dolphin leaping out of the water. Its two brightest stars carry the odd names Rotanev and Sualocin, which are 'Nicolaus Venator' spelled in reverse after the astronomer Niccolo Cacciatore.

constellations.name: Dorado
constellations.story: Dorado is the Dolphinfish, a southern constellation charted by Dutch navigators in the 1590s. It contains most of the Large Magellanic Cloud, the Milky Way's brightest satellite galaxy, and the Tarantula Nebula, a huge star-forming region. Its brightest star is Alpha Doradus, a blue-white star about 170 light-years away.

constellations.name: Draco
constellations.story: Draco is the Dragon, the serpent Ladon that guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides and was killed by Heracles. It winds around the north celestial pole and never sets from northern latitudes. Its star Thuban was the pole star around 3000 BC, and the constellation contains the Cat's Eye Nebula, a beautiful planetary nebula.

constellations.name: Equuleus
constellations.story: Equuleus is the Little Horse, the second-smallest constellation in the sky. It is one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy and traditionally represents a foal, sometimes linked to Celeris, the brother of Pegasus. It is faint, with only one star, Kitalpha, brighter than fourth magnitude.

constellations.name: Eridanus
constellations.story: Eridanus is the River, a vast winding stream of stars that begins near Orion and flows far into the southern sky. It is the sixth-largest constellation and contains Achernar, a rapidly spinning blue star at the river's end. In myth it is often identified with the Po, the river into which Phaethon fell after losing control of the Sun's chariot.

constellations.name: Fornax
constellations.story: Fornax is the Furnace, one of the faint southern constellations named by Lacaille after a chemical laboratory furnace. It is unremarkable to the eye, but it contains the Fornax Cluster of galaxies and the Fornax Dwarf galaxy. The Hubble Ultra Deep Field, one of the deepest images of the universe ever made, was taken in this constellation.

constellations.name: Gemini
constellations.story: Gemini is the Twins, usually identified as Castor and Pollux, the inseparable brothers of Greek myth who were placed in the sky together after Castor's death. Its brightest star, Pollux, is an orange giant with a confirmed exoplanet, while Castor is a remarkable six-star system. The Geminid meteor shower radiates from this constellation each December.

constellations.name: Grus
constellations.story: Grus is the Crane, one of the southern constellations introduced by Dutch navigators at the end of the 16th century. It is a fairly prominent southern spring constellation whose brightest star, Alnair, is a blue-white subgiant about 100 light-years away. It contains the Grus Quartet, a compact group of four galaxies.

constellations.name: Hercules
constellations.story: Hercules is the Strongman, the greatest of Greek heroes, shown kneeling with one foot on Draco's head. It is one of the largest constellations but has no first-magnitude star; its brightest is Kornephoros. It contains M13, the Great Globular Cluster, one of the finest in the northern sky.

constellations.name: Horologium
constellations.story: Horologium is the Pendulum Clock, a faint southern constellation introduced by Lacaille in the 18th century. It lies near the bright star Achernar but has no star above fourth magnitude. Its brightest star, Alpha Horologii, is a yellow giant about 115 light-years away.

constellations.name: Hydra
constellations.story: Hydra is the Water Snake, the largest constellation of all, stretching more than a quarter of the way around the sky. It represents the many-headed monster killed by Heracles, and its head lies south of Cancer while its tail reaches into Libra. Its brightest star, Alphard, has a name meaning 'the solitary one', and the constellation contains the spiral galaxy M83.

constellations.name: Hydrus
constellations.story: Hydrus is the Lesser Water Snake, a small southern constellation introduced by Dutch navigators in the 1590s. It lies near the south celestial pole and the Magellanic Clouds and has no ancient mythology of its own. Its brightest star, Beta Hydri, is a yellow star only about 24 light-years away.

constellations.name: Indus
constellations.story: Indus is the Indian, a southern constellation introduced by Dutch navigators in the 1590s to represent a person from the East Indies. It is faint and lies in a relatively empty part of the southern sky. Its brightest star, Alpha Indi, is an orange giant about 100 light-years away.

constellations.name: Lacerta
constellations.story: Lacerta is the Lizard, a faint northern constellation introduced by Hevelius in 1687. It lies inside the Milky Way between Cygnus and Andromeda and has no star brighter than fourth magnitude. Its brightest star, Alpha Lacertae, is a blue-white star about 100 light-years away.

constellations.name: Leo
constellations.story: Leo is the Lion, the Nemean Lion killed by Heracles as the first of his twelve labours. Its brightest star, Regulus, marks the lion's heart and spins so fast that it is noticeably flattened. The lion's mane forms the Sickle asterism, and the constellation contains the Leo Triplet of galaxies and the radiant of the Leonid meteor shower.

constellations.name: Leo Minor
constellations.story: Leo Minor is the Little Lion, a small faint constellation created by Hevelius in 1687 to fill a gap north of Leo. It has no star brighter than fourth magnitude; its brightest is Praecipua. It is one of several small northern constellations with no ancient mythology.

constellations.name: Lepus
constellations.story: Lepus is the Hare, crouched at the feet of Orion, where ancient star maps showed the hunter's dogs chasing it. It is a small constellation below Orion whose brightest star, Arneb, is a yellow-white supergiant. It contains M79, a globular cluster that is unusual for being found in the direction opposite the Milky Way's centre.

constellations.name: Libra
constellations.story: Libra is the Scales, the only zodiac constellation that represents an object rather than a living creature. In ancient Greece it was part of neighbouring Scorpius and marked the scorpion's claws; the star names Zubeneschamali and Zubenelgenubi still mean 'northern claw' and 'southern claw'. It has no first-magnitude star, its brightest being Zubeneschamali.

constellations.name: Lupus
constellations.story: Lupus is the Wolf, an ancient southern constellation listed by Ptolemy. It lies along the Milky Way between Centaurus and Scorpius and is full of faint stars and clusters. Its brightest star, Alpha Lupi, is a blue giant about 460 light-years away.

constellations.name: Lynx
constellations.story: Lynx is the Lynx, a faint northern constellation invented by Hevelius in 1687, who joked that only someone with lynx-like eyesight could see it. It contains no star brighter than third magnitude, though its brightest, Alpha Lyncis, is a red giant. The constellation lies between Ursa Major and Auriga.

constellations.name: Lyra
constellations.story: Lyra is the Lyre, the instrument of Orpheus, whose music could charm animals, rocks and even the gods. Its brightest star, Vega, is the fifth-brightest star in the night sky and the anchor of the Summer Triangle. The constellation contains the Ring Nebula and the double-double star Epsilon Lyrae, and the Lyrid meteor shower radiates from here each April.

constellations.name: Mensa
constellations.story: Mensa is Table Mountain, a faint southern constellation named by Lacaille after the mountain that overlooks Cape Town. It has the faintest brightest star of any constellation, Alpha Mensae at only fifth magnitude. Part of the Large Magellanic Cloud spills into its borders.

constellations.name: Microscopium
constellations.story: Microscopium is the Microscope, one of Lacaille's 18th-century scientific-instrument constellations in the southern sky. It is faint and compact, with no star brighter than fourth magnitude. Its brightest star, Gamma Microscopii, is a yellow giant.

constellations.name: Monoceros
constellations.story: Monoceros is the Unicorn, a faint equatorial constellation created by Petrus Plancius in the early 17th century. It lies inside the Milky Way and contains several notable objects, including the Rosette Nebula and the Christmas Tree Cluster. It has no star brighter than third magnitude, its brightest being Beta Monocerotis, a fine triple star.

constellations.name: Musca
constellations.story: Musca is the Fly, a small southern constellation introduced by Dutch navigators in the 1590s, originally called the Bee. It lies just south of Crux and contains the globular cluster NGC 4833. Its brightest star, Alpha Muscae, is a blue-white star about 315 light-years away.

constellations.name: Norma
constellations.story: Norma is the Carpenter's Square, a small southern constellation named by Lacaille after a measuring tool. It lies in the thick of the Milky Way and is rich in star clusters, though its brightest star, Gamma2 Normae, is only fourth magnitude. It is one of Lacaille's 14 southern constellations.

constellations.name: Octans
constellations.story: Octans is the Octant, a faint southern constellation named by Lacaille after the navigating instrument. It contains the south celestial pole, but the pole star itself is Sigma Octantis, a star barely visible to the naked eye. The constellation's brightest star is Nu Octantis, a yellow giant.

constellations.name: Ophiuchus
constellations.story: Ophiuchus is the Serpent Bearer, usually identified with Asclepius, the healer who learned how to raise the dead. It is the thirteenth constellation of the zodiac, even though it is not one of the traditional twelve: the Sun passes through it from late November to mid-December. It is large and contains the globular clusters M10 and M12, and Barnard's Star, one of the closest stars to the Sun.

constellations.name: Orion
constellations.story: Orion is the Hunter, the most recognisable winter constellation, with three belt stars in a line and bright Rigel and Betelgeuse on either side. It contains the Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery visible to the naked eye, and the Horsehead Nebula. In myth Orion was a giant hunter who boasted he could kill every animal on Earth.

constellations.name: Pavo
constellations.story: Pavo is the Peacock, a southern constellation introduced by Dutch navigators at the end of the 16th century. Its brightest star, Peacock, is a blue-white subgiant about 180 light-years away. It contains the globular cluster NGC 6752, one of the brightest in the sky.

constellations.name: Pegasus
constellations.story: Pegasus is the Winged Horse, born from the blood of Medusa and later ridden by Bellerophon. Its Great Square of four stars is a landmark of the autumn sky, though the star Alpheratz is formally shared with Andromeda. In 1995 the star 51 Pegasi became the first Sun-like star found to have a planet, and the constellation also contains the globular cluster M15.

constellations.name: Perseus
constellations.story: Perseus is the Hero, the slayer of Medusa who rescued Andromeda from the sea monster. Its brightest star, Mirfak, sits in a rich field of stars, and Algol is the famous eclipsing binary known since ancient times as the Demon Star. The constellation contains the Double Cluster and is the radiant of the Perseid meteor shower each August.

constellations.name: Phoenix
constellations.story: Phoenix is the mythical bird reborn from its ashes, one of the southern constellations introduced by Dutch navigators in the 1590s. Its brightest star, Ankaa, is an orange giant about 85 light-years away. It contains the Phoenix Dwarf galaxy, a small satellite of the Milky Way.

constellations.name: Pictor
constellations.story: Pictor is the Painter's Easel, a faint southern constellation introduced by Lacaille in the 18th century. It contains Beta Pictoris, a young star with a famous debris disk and at least one directly imaged planet. Its brightest star, Alpha Pictoris, is a blue-white star about 95 light-years away.

constellations.name: Pisces
constellations.story: Pisces is the Fishes, two fish tied together at the tail by a cord; in myth Aphrodite and Eros turned into fish to escape the monster Typhon. It is a faint zodiac constellation, but it holds the vernal equinox, the point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator each March. Its brightest star is Alpherg, an orange giant.

constellations.name: Piscis Austrinus
constellations.story: Piscis Austrinus is the Southern Fish, an ancient constellation shown drinking the water poured from Aquarius's jar. Its brightest star, Fomalhaut, is one of the four Royal Stars of ancient Persian astronomy and has a famous debris disk. Fomalhaut is a young star only about 25 light-years away.

constellations.name: Puppis
constellations.story: Puppis is the Stern, the stern section of the old constellation Argo Navis, the ship of the Argonauts. It lies in the southern Milky Way and is rich in open clusters, including M46, M47 and M93. Its brightest star, Naos, is a hot, extremely luminous blue supergiant.

constellations.name: Pyxis
constellations.story: Pyxis is the Mariner's Compass, a small faint constellation created by Lacaille from part of the old constellation Argo Navis. It represents the compass used to steer the ship of the Argonauts. Its brightest star, Alpha Pyxidis, is a blue giant about 880 light-years away.

constellations.name: Reticulum
constellations.story: Reticulum is the Reticle, a small southern constellation named by Lacaille after the crosshair eyepiece he used for measuring star positions. It is faint and lies near the Large Magellanic Cloud. Its brightest star, Alpha Reticuli, is a yellow giant about 160 light-years away.

constellations.name: Sagitta
constellations.story: Sagitta is the Arrow, the third-smallest constellation, usually identified with the arrow of Hercules or of Apollo. It flies through the Milky Way between Aquila and Cygnus and contains the globular cluster M71. Its brightest star, Gamma Sagittae, is an orange giant.

constellations.name: Sagittarius
constellations.story: Sagittarius is the Archer, a zodiac constellation whose main stars form the Teapot asterism. It points toward the centre of the Milky Way, which lies within its borders, so the constellation is crowded with clusters and nebulae including the Lagoon and Trifid nebulae. The supermassive black hole at the centre of our galaxy, Sagittarius A-star, takes its name from this constellation.

constellations.name: Scorpius
constellations.story: Scorpius is the Scorpion, the creature that killed Orion in Greek myth; the two constellations are placed on opposite sides of the sky so they never meet. Its brightest star, Antares, is a red supergiant whose name means 'rival of Mars' because of its colour. The constellation's curved tail contains the open clusters M6 and M7 and the bright star Shaula.

constellations.name: Sculptor
constellations.story: Sculptor is the Sculptor's Studio, a faint southern constellation introduced by Lacaille in the 18th century. It contains the Sculptor Galaxy, also called NGC 253, one of the brightest spiral galaxies in the sky, and the Sculptor Group of galaxies. Its brightest star, Alpha Sculptoris, is only fourth magnitude.

constellations.name: Scutum
constellations.story: Scutum is the Shield, a small constellation created by Hevelius in 1683 and named in honour of King John III Sobieski of Poland after his victory at Vienna. It lies in a bright star cloud of the Milky Way and contains the Wild Duck Cluster, M11. Its brightest star, Alpha Scuti, is an orange giant.

constellations.name: Serpens
constellations.story: Serpens is the Serpent, the snake held by Ophiuchus and a symbol of healing and rebirth. It is the only constellation split into two separate pieces, Serpens Caput (the head) and Serpens Cauda (the tail), with Ophiuchus between them. The tail contains the Eagle Nebula with the Pillars of Creation, while the head contains the globular cluster M5.

constellations.name: Sextans
constellations.story: Sextans is the Sextant, a faint equatorial constellation created by Hevelius in 1687 and named after the instrument he used to measure star positions. It lies south of Leo and has no star brighter than fourth magnitude. Its brightest star, Alpha Sextantis, is a blue-white star about 290 light-years away.

constellations.name: Taurus
constellations.story: Taurus is the Bull, often identified with Zeus in disguise as he carried off Europa. Its brightest star, Aldebaran, marks the bull's eye and is an orange giant, while the V-shaped Hyades cluster forms its face. The constellation also contains the Pleiades, the Crab Nebula, and the radiant of the Taurid meteor shower.

constellations.name: Telescopium
constellations.story: Telescopium is the Telescope, one of Lacaille's faint southern constellations from the 18th century. It lies south of Sagittarius and has no star brighter than third magnitude. Its brightest star, Alpha Telescopii, is a blue-white subgiant about 280 light-years away.

constellations.name: Triangulum
constellations.story: Triangulum is the Triangle, a small northern constellation known since ancient times. It contains M33, the Triangulum Galaxy, the third-largest galaxy in the Local Group and one of the most distant objects visible to the naked eye under very dark skies. Its brightest star is Beta Trianguli.

constellations.name: Triangulum Australe
constellations.story: Triangulum Australe is the Southern Triangle, one of the constellations introduced by Dutch navigators at the end of the 16th century. It lies in a bright part of the southern Milky Way, and its three main stars are all brighter than third magnitude. Its brightest star, Atria, is an orange giant about 390 light-years away.

constellations.name: Tucana
constellations.story: Tucana is the Toucan, a southern constellation introduced by Dutch navigators in the 1590s. It contains most of the Small Magellanic Cloud and 47 Tucanae, the second-brightest globular cluster in the sky after Omega Centauri. Its brightest star, Alpha Tucanae, is an orange giant about 200 light-years away.

constellations.name: Ursa Major
constellations.story: Ursa Major is the Great Bear, home to the Big Dipper, the best-known star pattern in the northern sky. The two stars at the end of the Dipper's bowl point to Polaris, and the bear's paws contain the galaxies M81 and M82, while M101, the Pinwheel Galaxy, lies near its tail. In myth the bear is Callisto, transformed by a jealous Hera.

constellations.name: Ursa Minor
constellations.story: Ursa Minor is the Little Bear, whose most famous star, Polaris, sits almost exactly above Earth's north pole and has guided travellers for centuries. Its stars form the Little Dipper, and because Earth's axis wobbles, Polaris has not always been the pole star and will not always be. The constellation also contains Kochab and Pherkad, the so-called Guardians of the Pole.

constellations.name: Vela
constellations.story: Vela is the Sails, part of the old constellation Argo Navis, the ship of the Argonauts, which was divided into three constellations in the 18th century. Its brightest star, Regor, is a hot supergiant, and the constellation contains the Vela supernova remnant, the Vela pulsar, and the Gum Nebula. The Vela pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star left by a supernova about 11,000 years ago.

constellations.name: Virgo
constellations.story: Virgo is the Maiden, usually identified with Astraea, the goddess of justice, or with Demeter, the harvest goddess; Spica, its brightest star, is an ear of wheat in her hand. It is the second-largest constellation and contains the Virgo Cluster, a vast collection of galaxies at the heart of the Local Supercluster. Spica is a hot blue binary star about 250 light-years away.

constellations.name: Volans
constellations.story: Volans is the Flying Fish, a small southern constellation introduced by Dutch navigators in the 1590s. It lies near the Large Magellanic Cloud but contains no bright stars; its brightest is Beta Volantis, an orange giant. The name reflects the flying fish that sailors saw gliding above the waves.

constellations.name: Vulpecula
constellations.story: Vulpecula is the Little Fox, a faint northern constellation created by Hevelius in 1687; it originally carried a goose, and the star Anser still recalls that goose. It contains the Dumbbell Nebula, M27, one of the brightest planetary nebulae in the sky, and the Coathanger cluster. Its brightest star is Anser.
